days.title: The Boarding House — part 1: a calculated intervention
days.challenge: Separate the narrator’s account, social conventions and a character’s strategic reasoning.
days.focus: Honor as protection and bargaining power.
days.context: Mrs. Mooney runs a boarding house. After allowing her daughter Polly’s relationship with a lodger to develop, she prepares to intervene.
days.contentNote: Domestic violence in the backstory and a sexual relationship interpreted through restrictive social conventions.

excerpt.locator: The Boarding House; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 1–11; opens “Mrs. Mooney was a butcher's daughter. She was a woman who was quite able to keep things to herself: ”; closes “fied her and she thought of some mothers she knew who could not get their daughters off their hands.”.

blocks.text: Mrs. Mooney was a butcher's daughter. She was a woman who was quite able to keep things to herself: a determined woman. She had married her father's foreman and opened a butcher's shop near Spring Gardens. But as soon as his father-in-law was dead Mr. Mooney began to go to the devil. He drank, plundered the till, ran headlong into debt. It was no use making him take the pledge: he was sure to break out again a few days after. By fighting his wife in the presence of customers and by buying bad meat he ruined his business. One night he went for his wife with the cleaver and she had to sleep in a neighbour's house.

After that they lived apart. She went to the priest and got a separation from him with care of the children. She would give him neither money nor food nor house-room; and so he was obliged to enlist himself as a sheriff's man. He was a shabby stooped little drunkard with a white face and a white moustache and white eyebrows, pencilled above his little eyes, which were pink-veined and raw; and all day long he sat in the bailiff's room, waiting to be put on a job. Mrs. Mooney, who had taken what remained of her money out of the butcher business and set up a boarding-house in Hardwicke Street, was a big imposing woman. Her house had a floating population made up of tourists from Liverpool and the Isle of Man and, occasionally, artistes from the music halls. Its resident population was made up of clerks from the city. She governed the house cunningly and firmly, knew when to give credit, when to be stern and when to let things pass. All the resident young men spoke of her as The Madam.

Mrs. Mooney's young men paid fifteen shillings a week for board and lodgings (beer or stout at dinner excluded). They shared in common tastes and occupations and for this reason they were very chummy with one another. They discussed with one another the chances of favourites and outsiders. Jack Mooney, the Madam's son, who was clerk to a commission agent in Fleet Street, had the reputation of being a hard case. He was fond of using soldiers' obscenities: usually he came home in the small hours. When he met his friends he had always a good one to tell them and he was always sure to be on to a good thing—that is to say, a likely horse or a likely artiste. He was also handy with the mits and sang comic songs. On Sunday nights there would often be a reunion in Mrs. Mooney's front drawing-room. The music-hall artistes would oblige; and Sheridan played waltzes and polkas and vamped accompaniments. Polly Mooney, the Madam's daughter, would also sing. She sang:

"I'm a . . . naughty girl.
You needn't sham:
You know I am."

Polly was a slim girl of nineteen; she had light soft hair and a small full mouth. Her eyes, which were grey with a shade of green through them, had a habit of glancing upwards when she spoke with anyone, which made her look like a little perverse madonna. Mrs. Mooney had first sent her daughter to be a typist in a corn-factor's office but, as a disreputable sheriff's man used to come every other day to the office, asking to be allowed to say a word to his daughter, she had taken her daughter home again and set her to do housework. As Polly was very lively the intention was to give her the run of the young men. Besides, young men like to feel that there is a young woman not very far away. Polly, of course, flirted with the young men but Mrs. Mooney, who was a shrewd judge, knew that the young men were only passing the time away: none of them meant business. Things went on so for a long time and Mrs. Mooney began to think of sending Polly back to typewriting when she noticed that something was going on between Polly and one of the young men. She watched the pair and kept her own counsel.

Polly knew that she was being watched, but still her mother's persistent silence could not be misunderstood. There had been no open complicity between mother and daughter, no open understanding but, though people in the house began to talk of the affair, still Mrs. Mooney did not intervene. Polly began to grow a little strange in her manner and the young man was evidently perturbed. At last, when she judged it to be the right moment, Mrs. Mooney intervened. She dealt with moral problems as a cleaver deals with meat: and in this case she had made up her mind.

It was a bright Sunday morning of early summer, promising heat, but with a fresh breeze blowing. All the windows of the boarding house were open and the lace curtains ballooned gently towards the street beneath the raised sashes. The belfry of George's Church sent out constant peals and worshippers, singly or in groups, traversed the little circus before the church, revealing their purpose by their self-contained demeanour no less than by the little volumes in their gloved hands. Breakfast was over in the boarding house and the table of the breakfast-room was covered with plates on which lay yellow streaks of eggs with morsels of bacon-fat and bacon-rind. Mrs. Mooney sat in the straw arm-chair and watched the servant Mary remove the breakfast things. She made Mary collect the crusts and pieces of broken bread to help to make Tuesday's bread-pudding. When the table was cleared, the broken bread collected, the sugar and butter safe under lock and key, she began to reconstruct the interview which she had had the night before with Polly. Things were as she had suspected: she had been frank in her questions and Polly had been frank in her answers. Both had been somewhat awkward, of course. She had been made awkward by her not wishing to receive the news in too cavalier a fashion or to seem to have connived and Polly had been made awkward not merely because allusions of that kind always made her awkward but also because she did not wish it to be thought that in her wise innocence she had divined the intention behind her mother's tolerance.

Mrs. Mooney glanced instinctively at the little gilt clock on the mantelpiece as soon as she had become aware through her revery that the bells of George's Church had stopped ringing. It was seventeen minutes past eleven: she would have lots of time to have the matter out with Mr. Doran and then catch short twelve at Marlborough Street. She was sure she would win. To begin with she had all the weight of social opinion on her side: she was an outraged mother. She had allowed him to live beneath her roof, assuming that he was a man of honour, and he had simply abused her hospitality. He was thirty-four or thirty-five years of age, so that youth could not be pleaded as his excuse; nor could ignorance be his excuse since he was a man who had seen something of the world. He had simply taken advantage of Polly's youth and inexperience: that was evident. The question was: What reparation would he make?

There must be reparation made in such case. It is all very well for the man: he can go his ways as if nothing had happened, having had his moment of pleasure, but the girl has to bear the brunt. Some mothers would be content to patch up such an affair for a sum of money; she had known cases of it. But she would not do so. For her only one reparation could make up for the loss of her daughter's honour: marriage.

She counted all her cards again before sending Mary up to Mr. Doran's room to say that she wished to speak with him. She felt sure she would win. He was a serious young man, not rakish or loud-voiced like the others. If it had been Mr. Sheridan or Mr. Meade or Bantam Lyons her task would have been much harder. She did not think he would face publicity. All the lodgers in the house knew something of the affair; details had been invented by some. Besides, he had been employed for thirteen years in a great Catholic wine-merchant's office and publicity would mean for him, perhaps, the loss of his job. Whereas if he agreed all might be well. She knew he had a good screw for one thing and she suspected he had a bit of stuff put by.

Nearly the half-hour! She stood up and surveyed herself in the pier-glass. The decisive expression of her great florid face satisfied her and she thought of some mothers she knew who could not get their daughters off their hands.

questions.prompt: How does the cleaver comparison connect Mrs. Mooney’s past to her approach to moral problems?
facilitatorNotes: Her history in a butcher’s business becomes a figure for decisive cutting through ambiguity. It suggests practical strength but also a potentially brutal simplification.
evidence: She dealt with moral problems as a cleaver deals with meat

questions.prompt: What is the force of the claim that there was no open complicity?
facilitatorNotes: The qualifier open preserves a tacit understanding while denying explicit agreement. Readers must distinguish inferred coordination from a stated plan.
evidence: There had been no open complicity between mother and daughter

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Mooney’s account combine a real social inequality with a strategy for winning?
facilitatorNotes: She notes that a woman bears more reputational cost, yet calculates Doran’s job, savings and fear of publicity. Protection and self-interested bargaining are both present.
evidence: the girl has to bear the brunt.

days.title: The Boarding House — part 2: what is left offstage
days.challenge: Compare shifting viewpoints and an ending that withholds the decisive conversation.
days.focus: Coercion, agency and the limits of inferred agreement.
days.context: Mrs. Mooney has summoned Doran. The story now follows his anxiety, then Polly’s changing state as she waits.
days.contentNote: Sexual reputation, coercion, threats of violence and a character’s statement about self-harm.

excerpt.locator: The Boarding House; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 12–30; opens “Mr. Doran was very anxious indeed this Sunday morning. He had made two attempts to shave but his han”; closes “Then she remembered what she had been waiting for.”.

blocks.text: Mr. Doran was very anxious indeed this Sunday morning. He had made two attempts to shave but his hand had been so unsteady that he had been obliged to desist. Three days' reddish beard fringed his jaws and every two or three minutes a mist gathered on his glasses so that he had to take them off and polish them with his pocket-handkerchief. The recollection of his confession of the night before was a cause of acute pain to him; the priest had drawn out every ridiculous detail of the affair and in the end had so magnified his sin that he was almost thankful at being afforded a loophole of reparation. The harm was done. What could he do now but marry her or run away? He could not brazen it out. The affair would be sure to be talked of and his employer would be certain to hear of it. Dublin is such a small city: everyone knows everyone else's business. He felt his heart leap warmly in his throat as he heard in his excited imagination old Mr. Leonard calling out in his rasping voice: "Send Mr. Doran here, please."

All his long years of service gone for nothing! All his industry and diligence thrown away! As a young man he had sown his wild oats, of course; he had boasted of his free-thinking and denied the existence of God to his companions in public-houses. But that was all passed and done with . . . nearly. He still bought a copy of Reynolds's Newspaper every week but he attended to his religious duties and for nine-tenths of the year lived a regular life. He had money enough to settle down on; it was not that. But the family would look down on her. First of all there was her disreputable father and then her mother's boarding house was beginning to get a certain fame. He had a notion that he was being had. He could imagine his friends talking of the affair and laughing. She was a little vulgar; sometimes she said "I seen" and "If I had've known." But what would grammar matter if he really loved her? He could not make up his mind whether to like her or despise her for what she had done. Of course he had done it too. His instinct urged him to remain free, not to marry. Once you are married you are done for, it said.

While he was sitting helplessly on the side of the bed in shirt and trousers she tapped lightly at his door and entered. She told him all, that she had made a clean breast of it to her mother and that her mother would speak with him that morning. She cried and threw her arms round his neck, saying:
"O Bob! Bob! What am I to do? What am I to do at all?"

She would put an end to herself, she said. He comforted her feebly, telling her not to cry, that it would be all right, never fear. He felt against his shirt the agitation of her bosom. It was not altogether his fault that it had happened. He remembered well, with the curious patient memory of the celibate, the first casual caresses her dress, her breath, her fingers had given him. Then late one night as he was undressing for bed she had tapped at his door, timidly. She wanted to relight her candle at his for hers had been blown out by a gust. It was her bath night. She wore a loose open combingjacket of printed flannel. Her white instep shone in the opening of her furry slippers and the blood glowed warmly behind her perfumed skin. From her hands and wrists too as she lit and steadied her candle a faint perfume arose.

On nights when he came in very late it was she who warmed up his dinner. He scarcely knew what he was eating feeling her beside him alone, at night, in the sleeping house. And her thoughtfulness! If the night was anyway cold or wet or windy there was sure to be a little tumbler of punch ready for him. Perhaps they could be happy together. . . .

They used to go upstairs together on tiptoe, each with a candle, and on the third landing exchange reluctant good-nights. They used to kiss. He remembered well her eyes, the touch of her hand and his delirium. . . .

But delirium passes. He echoed her phrase, applying it to himself: "What am I to do?" The instinct of the celibate warned him to hold back. But the sin was there; even his sense of honour told him that reparation must be made for such a sin.

While he was sitting with her on the side of the bed Mary came to the door and said that the missus wanted to see him in the parlour. He stood up to put on his coat and waistcoat, more helpless than ever. When he was dressed he went over to her to comfort her. It would be all right, never fear. He left her crying on the bed and moaning softly: "O my God!"

Going down the stairs his glasses became so dimmed with moisture that he had to take them off and polish them. He longed to ascend through the roof and fly away to another country where he would never hear again of his trouble, and yet a force pushed him downstairs step by step. The implacable faces of his employer and of the Madam stared upon his discomfiture. On the last flight of stairs he passed Jack Mooney who was coming up from the pantry nursing two bottles of Bass. They saluted coldly; and the lover's eyes rested for a second or two on a thick bulldog face and a pair of thick short arms. When he reached the foot of the staircase he glanced up and saw Jack regarding him from the door of the return-room.

Suddenly he remembered the night when one of the music-hall artistes, a little blond Londoner, had made a rather free allusion to Polly. The reunion had been almost broken up on account of Jack's violence. Everyone tried to quiet him. The music-hall artiste, a little paler than usual, kept smiling and saying that there was no harm meant: but Jack kept shouting at him that if any fellow tried that sort of a game on with his sister he'd bloody well put his teeth down his throat, so he would.

Polly sat for a little time on the side of the bed, crying. Then she dried her eyes and went over to the looking-glass. She dipped the end of the towel in the water-jug and refreshed her eyes with the cool water. She looked at herself in profile and readjusted a hairpin above her ear. Then she went back to the bed again and sat at the foot. She regarded the pillows for a long time and the sight of them awakened in her mind secret, amiable memories. She rested the nape of her neck against the cool iron bed-rail and fell into a revery. There was no longer any perturbation visible on her face.

She waited on patiently, almost cheerfully, without alarm, her memories gradually giving place to hopes and visions of the future. Her hopes and visions were so intricate that she no longer saw the white pillows on which her gaze was fixed or remembered that she was waiting for anything.
At last she heard her mother calling. She started to her feet and ran to the banisters.
"Polly! Polly!"
"Yes, mamma?"
"Come down, dear. Mr. Doran wants to speak to you."
Then she remembered what she had been waiting for.

questions.prompt: How do Doran’s objections reveal both social pressure and his own prejudice?
facilitatorNotes: Fear for his job and public standing creates pressure; contempt for Polly’s grammar and family shows class prejudice. He also admits his participation, undermining a simple account of innocent entrapment.
evidence: Of course he had done it too.

questions.prompt: What does the staircase scene make physically visible about his apparent choice?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines upward escape but is pushed downward by social obligation and the threatening presence of Jack. Spatial movement turns abstract pressure into a staged descent.
evidence: a force pushed him downstairs step by step.

questions.prompt: Why end before readers hear Mrs. Mooney’s conversation with Doran?
facilitatorNotes: The omission makes us infer an arrangement from Polly’s summons and changing mood. It keeps the precise terms, Doran’s consent and Polly’s expectations from becoming settled facts.
evidence: Then she remembered what she had been waiting for.

days.title: Easter, 1916
days.challenge: Hold praise, personal dislike and political doubt together across a recurring refrain.
days.focus: Commemoration that refuses to become uncomplicated endorsement.
days.context: Yeats responds to the Irish Easter Rising and the deaths of its leaders. The speaker revisits people he once knew in ordinary social life; the poem itself does not supply a full history of the rising.
days.contentNote: Political violence, execution and mourning; the speaker also judges a woman’s political voice through gendered expectations.

excerpt.locator: Easter, 1916; complete individual work; opens “I have met them at close of day Coming with vivid faces From counter or desk among grey Eighteenth-c”; closes “ and in time to be, Wherever green is worn. Are changed, changed utterly: A terrible beauty is born.”.

blocks.text:
I have met them at close of day
Coming with vivid faces
From counter or desk among grey
Eighteenth-century houses.
I have passed with a nod of the head
Or polite meaningless words,
Or have lingered awhile and said
Polite meaningless words,
And thought before I had done
Of a mocking tale or a gibe
To please a companion
Around the fire at the club,
Being certain that they and I
But lived where motley is worn:
All changed, changed utterly:
A terrible beauty is born.

That woman’s days were spent
In ignorant good will,
Her nights in argument
Until her voice grew shrill.
What voice more sweet than hers
When young and beautiful,
She rode to harriers?
This man had kept a school
And rode our winged horse.
This other his helper and friend
Was coming into his force;
He might have won fame in the end,
So sensitive his nature seemed,
So daring and sweet his thought.
This other man I had dreamed
A drunken, vain-glorious lout.
He had done most bitter wrong
To some who are near my heart,
Yet I number him in the song;
He, too, has resigned his part
In the casual comedy;
He, too, has been changed in his turn,
Transformed utterly:
A terrible beauty is born.

Hearts with one purpose alone
Through summer and winter seem
Enchanted to a stone
To trouble the living stream.
The horse that comes from the road.
The rider, the birds that range
From cloud to tumbling cloud,
Minute by minute change;
A shadow of cloud on the stream
Changes minute by minute;
A horse-hoof slides on the brim,
And a horse plashes within it
Where long-legged moor-hens dive,
And hens to moor-cocks call.
Minute by minute they live:
The stone’s in the midst of all.

Too long a sacrifice
Can make a stone of the heart.
O when may it suffice?
That is heaven’s part, our part
To murmur name upon name.
As a mother names her child
When sleep at last has come
On limbs that had run wild.
What is it but nightfall?
No, no, not night but death;
Was it needless death after all?
For England may keep faith
For all that is done and said.
We know their dream; enough
To know they dreamed and are dead.
And what if excess of love
Bewildered them till they died?
I write it out in a verse—
MacDonagh and MacBride
And Connolly and Pearse
Now and in time to be,
Wherever green is worn.
Are changed, changed utterly:
A terrible beauty is born.

questions.prompt: How does the repetition of polite meaningless words prepare for the refrain about change?
facilitatorNotes: Ordinary encounters initially seem trivial and theatrical; death retrospectively transforms their significance. The speaker’s earlier certainty becomes part of what must change.
evidence: Polite meaningless words,

questions.prompt: Is the stone an image of admirable steadfastness, dangerous rigidity, or both?
facilitatorNotes: A single purpose resists the living stream’s continual change. The later stone of the heart explicitly warns that sacrifice may harden feeling, while endurance remains impressive.
evidence:
Too long a sacrifice
Can make a stone of the heart.

questions.prompt: Why preserve the question about needless death even while writing the names into verse?
facilitatorNotes: Commemoration need not settle the political necessity of the sacrifice. The refrain’s terrible beauty binds admiration to cost, and naming acknowledges persons without erasing doubt.
evidence: Was it needless death after all?

days.title: Sixteen Dead Men
days.challenge: Track an imagined dialogue between living political calculation and the authority of the dead.
days.focus: The emotional consequences of execution for public argument.
days.context: The poem responds to executed Irish rebels during the First World War. Its addressed opponent proposes waiting until Germany is defeated; the speaker asks whether that reasoning can still command attention.
days.contentNote: Execution and the political afterlife of the dead.

excerpt.locator: Sixteen Dead Men; complete individual work; opens “O but we talked at large before The sixteen men were shot, But who can talk of give and take, What s”; closes “ have found Lord Edward and Wolfe Tone, Or meddle with our give and take That converse bone to bone.”.

blocks.text:
O but we talked at large before
The sixteen men were shot,
But who can talk of give and take,
What should be and what not?
While those dead men are loitering there
To stir the boiling pot.

You say that we should still the land
Till Germany’s overcome;
But who is there to argue that
Now Pearse is deaf and dumb?
And is their logic to outweigh
MacDonagh’s bony thumb?

How could you dream they’d listen
That have an ear alone
For those new comrades they have found
Lord Edward and Wolfe Tone,
Or meddle with our give and take
That converse bone to bone.

questions.prompt: How does the boiling pot change the force of the opening talk of give and take?
facilitatorNotes: Negotiation sounds measured, while the dead are imagined as continuing to intensify public feeling. The image makes execution an active political force after bodily death.
evidence: To stir the boiling pot.

questions.prompt: Why oppose logic to a bony thumb rather than to another argument?
facilitatorNotes: The bodily remnant makes sacrifice resistant to ordinary debate. It can suggest the power of memory and the danger that emotionally authoritative symbols displace reasoning.
evidence: MacDonagh’s bony thumb?

questions.prompt: What does the final conversation bone to bone imply about the audience for compromise?
facilitatorNotes: The dead are imagined joining earlier rebels in a historical community beyond current bargaining. The living speaker cannot simply negotiate with that symbolic conversation.
evidence: That converse bone to bone.

days.title: The Rose Tree
days.challenge: Evaluate a symbolic argument whose apparent necessity depends on its premises.
days.focus: The rhetoric of sacrificial violence.
days.context: Yeats stages an imagined exchange between Pearse and Connolly. This is a lyric dialogue, not a transcript of their words.
days.contentNote: An imagined argument for political blood sacrifice; examine its rhetoric rather than treating it as an instruction.

excerpt.locator: The Rose Tree; complete individual work; opens ““O words are lightly spoken” Said Pearse to Connolly, “Maybe a breath of politic words Has withered ”; closes “hed away? O plain as plain can be There’s nothing but our own red blood Can make a right Rose Tree.””.

blocks.text:
“O words are lightly spoken”
Said Pearse to Connolly,
“Maybe a breath of politic words
Has withered our Rose Tree;
Or maybe but a wind that blows
Across the bitter sea.”

“It needs to be but watered,”
James Connolly replied,
“To make the green come out again
And spread on every side,
And shake the blossom from the bud
To be the garden’s pride.”

“But where can we draw water”
Said Pearse to Connolly,
“When all the wells are parched away?
O plain as plain can be
There’s nothing but our own red blood
Can make a right Rose Tree.”

questions.prompt: What possible causes of the rose tree’s decline are offered before the proposed remedy?
facilitatorNotes: Empty political language and a hostile wind from across the sea offer internal and external explanations. Maybe marks uncertainty that the ending later suppresses.
evidence: Maybe a breath of politic words

questions.prompt: What does Connolly’s gardening language promise?
facilitatorNotes: Water would restore green growth, bloom and communal pride. The natural cycle makes restoration appear both desirable and potentially simple.
evidence: To make the green come out again

questions.prompt: Which unproved premise makes blood appear to be the only remaining answer?
facilitatorNotes: All wells are said to be dry, eliminating ordinary water. Plain as plain claims obviousness, but the metaphor does not demonstrate that political alternatives are exhausted or sacrifice effective.
evidence: When all the wells are parched away?

days.title: On a Political Prisoner
days.challenge: Distinguish reported action, rhetorical questioning and idealized memory.
days.focus: Who controls the meaning of a woman’s political transformation.
days.context: A speaker imagines an imprisoned woman’s patience with a gull and recalls her earlier outdoor life. Notice how much of the account is supplied by the observer.
days.contentNote: Political imprisonment and a speaker’s hostile judgment of political activism.

excerpt.locator: On a Political Prisoner; complete individual work; opens “She that but little patience knew, From childhood on, had now so much A grey gull lost its fear and ”; closes “ stare Upon the cloudy canopy, While under its storm-beaten breast Cried out the hollows of the sea.”.

blocks.text:
She that but little patience knew,
From childhood on, had now so much
A grey gull lost its fear and flew
Down to her cell and there alit,
And there endured her fingers touch
And from her fingers ate its bit.

Did she in touching that lone wing
Recall the years before her mind
Became a bitter, an abstract thing,
Her thought some popular enmity:
Blind and leader of the blind
Drinking the foul ditch where they lie?

When long ago I saw her ride
Under Ben Bulban to the meet,
The beauty of her country-side
With all youth’s lonely wildness stirred,
She seemed to have grown clean and sweet
Like any rock-bred, sea-borne bird:

Sea-borne, or balanced on the air
When first it sprang out of the nest
Upon some lofty rock to stare
Upon the cloudy canopy,
While under its storm-beaten breast
Cried out the hollows of the sea.

questions.prompt: What specific behavior supports the claim that imprisonment has changed her patience?
facilitatorNotes: The gull loses fear, tolerates touch and feeds from her fingers. These actions imply sustained quiet attention, although the poem supplies no access to her own explanation.
evidence: A grey gull lost its fear and flew

questions.prompt: Does the question beginning Did she establish what the prisoner remembered?
facilitatorNotes: No. It projects the speaker’s preferred contrast between youthful beauty and abstract political enmity. The question form exposes the distance between speculation and testimony.
evidence: Did she in touching that lone wing

questions.prompt: How does the final bird comparison complicate the opening captive scene?
facilitatorNotes: The remembered rider becomes a bird at the edge of flight over a turbulent sea; the prison gull links captivity with an image of freedom. Readers can find admiration while also questioning the speaker’s idealization.
evidence: Like any rock-bred, sea-borne bird:

days.title: The Leaders of the Crowd
days.challenge: Follow an argument that turns critically upon its own preferred alternative.
days.focus: Accusation, solitary inquiry and the attractions of collective life.
days.context: Helicon invokes the traditional mountain of poetic inspiration. The poem opposes rumor to scholarship, then complicates that opposition in its final lines.

excerpt.locator: The Leaders of the Crowd; complete individual work; opens “They must to keep their certainty accuse All that are different of a base intent; Pull down establis”; closes “y come. They have loud music, hope every day renewed And heartier loves; that lamp is from the tomb.”.

blocks.text:
They must to keep their certainty accuse
All that are different of a base intent;
Pull down established honour; hawk for news
Whatever their loose phantasy invent
And murmur it with bated breath, as though
The abounding gutter had been Helicon
Or calumny a song. How can they know
Truth flourishes where the student’s lamp has shone,
And there alone, that have no solitude?
So the crowd come they care not what may come.
They have loud music, hope every day renewed
And heartier loves; that lamp is from the tomb.

questions.prompt: Why does the opening make accusation necessary to the leaders’ certainty?
facilitatorNotes: They preserve certainty by assigning base motives to difference, insulating belief from challenge. The poem locates a psychological function behind public denunciation.
evidence: They must to keep their certainty accuse

questions.prompt: How does the gutter/Helicon comparison attack both information and art?
facilitatorNotes: Rumor is treated as news and slander as song; degraded material is falsely elevated into cultural authority. The contrast tests the sources that support public conviction.
evidence: Or calumny a song.

questions.prompt: Why does the lamp from the tomb prevent an easy victory for the solitary student?
facilitatorNotes: The crowd retains music, renewed hope and warmer love, while scholarship’s lamp is associated with death. The ending gives the rejected side human attractions and questions the cost of withdrawal.
evidence: And heartier loves; that lamp is from the tomb.

days.title: The Second Coming
days.challenge: Track how a confident announcement becomes a disturbing, unfinished question.
days.focus: Historical crisis and the instability of prophetic interpretation.
days.context: The poem uses Christian expectations of a second coming but gives the speaker a radically different vision. Spiritus Mundi names a world-spirit or shared store of images within the poem’s imaginative system.
days.contentNote: Apocalyptic violence and imagery of cultural collapse.

excerpt.locator: The Second Coming; complete individual work; opens “Turning and turning in the widening gyre The falcon cannot hear the falconer; Things fall apart; the”; closes “ng cradle, And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?”.

blocks.text:
Surely some revelation is at hand;
Surely the Second Coming is at hand.
The Second Coming! Hardly are those words out
When a vast image out of Spiritus Mundi
Troubles my sight: a waste of desert sand;
A shape with lion body and the head of a man,
A gaze blank and pitiless as the sun,
Is moving its slow thighs, while all about it
Wind shadows of the indignant desert birds.
The darkness drops again but now I know
That twenty centuries of stony sleep
Were vexed to nightmare by a rocking cradle,
And what rough beast, its hour come round at last,
Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?

questions.prompt: What relation breaks in the falcon image, and how does it prepare the widening political claims?
facilitatorNotes: The creature can no longer hear its guiding human voice. Expanding circular motion represents a loss of communication and control before the poem asserts general disorder.
evidence: The falcon cannot hear the falconer;

questions.prompt: How does the repeated Surely expose the speaker’s effort to make sense of disorder?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition sounds assured but insists on an interpretation not yet seen. The image that follows troubles rather than confirms the expected Christian revelation.
evidence: Surely some revelation is at hand;

questions.prompt: Why end with a question about birth instead of an account of arrival?
facilitatorNotes: The beast is approaching an ominous future whose meaning remains unresolved. Bethlehem and the cradle invert a familiar salvation story; the question withholds a stable final prophecy.
evidence: Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?

days.title: A Prayer for My Daughter
days.challenge: Evaluate a protective prayer that also prescribes another person’s life.
days.focus: Care, gender, custom and the wish for inward freedom.
days.context: A father hears a storm while his child sleeps. His hopes range from kindness and friendship to restrictions on beauty, opinion and place.
days.contentNote: Gendered expectations and mythological judgments about women are part of the speaker’s argument, open to criticism.

excerpt.locator: A Prayer for My Daughter; complete individual work; opens “Once more the storm is howling and half hid Under this cradle-hood and coverlid My child sleeps on. ”; closes “ence and beauty born? Ceremony’s a name for the rich horn. And custom for the spreading laurel tree.”.

blocks.text:
Once more the storm is howling and half hid
Under this cradle-hood and coverlid
My child sleeps on. There is no obstacle
But Gregory’s Wood and one bare hill
Whereby the haystack and roof-levelling wind,
Bred on the Atlantic, can be stayed;
And for an hour I have walked and prayed
Because of the great gloom that is in my mind.

I have walked and prayed for this young child an hour
And heard the sea-wind scream upon the tower,
And under the arches of the bridge, and scream
In the elms above the flooded stream;
Imagining in excited reverie
That the future years had come,
Dancing to a frenzied drum,
Out of the murderous innocence of the sea.

May she be granted beauty and yet not
Beauty to make a stranger’s eye distraught,
Or hers before a looking-glass, for such,
Being made beautiful overmuch,
Consider beauty a sufficient end,
Lose natural kindness and maybe
The heart-revealing intimacy
That chooses right and never find a friend.

Helen being chosen found life flat and dull
And later had much trouble from a fool,
While that great Queen, that rose out of the spray,
Being fatherless could have her way
Yet chose a bandy-legged smith for man.
It’s certain that fine women eat
A crazy salad with their meat
Whereby the Horn of Plenty is undone.

In courtesy I’d have her chiefly learned;
Hearts are not had as a gift but hearts are earned
By those that are not entirely beautiful;
Yet many, that have played the fool
For beauty’s very self, has charm made wise,
And many a poor man that has roved,
Loved and thought himself beloved,
From a glad kindness cannot take his eyes.

May she become a flourishing hidden tree
That all her thoughts may like the linnet be,
And have no business but dispensing round
Their magnanimities of sound,
Nor but in merriment begin a chase,
Nor but in merriment a quarrel.
Oh, may she live like some green laurel
Rooted in one dear perpetual place.

My mind, because the minds that I have loved,
The sort of beauty that I have approved,
Prosper but little, has dried up of late,
Yet knows that to be choked with hate
May well be of all evil chances chief.
If there’s no hatred in a mind
Assault and battery of the wind
Can never tear the linnet from the leaf.

An intellectual hatred is the worst,
So let her think opinions are accursed.
Have I not seen the loveliest woman born
Out of the mouth of Plenty’s horn,
Because of her opinionated mind
Barter that horn and every good
By quiet natures understood
For an old bellows full of angry wind?

Considering that, all hatred driven hence,
The soul recovers radical innocence
And learns at last that it is self-delighting,
Self-appeasing, self-affrighting.
And that its own sweet will is heaven’s will;
She can, though every face should scowl
And every windy quarter howl
Or every bellows burst, be happy still.

And may her bride-groom bring her to a house
Where all’s accustomed, ceremonious;
For arrogance and hatred are the wares
Peddled in the thoroughfares.
How but in custom and in ceremony
Are innocence and beauty born?
Ceremony’s a name for the rich horn.
And custom for the spreading laurel tree.

questions.prompt: How does the storm operate as both physical event and imagined history?
facilitatorNotes: Wind threatens roof and landscape, while the speaker imagines future years dancing violently. The cradle makes broad historical fear immediate and domestic.
evidence: Out of the murderous innocence of the sea.

questions.prompt: What is appealing and what is restrictive in the wish that the daughter become a hidden tree?
facilitatorNotes: Rootedness, generous song and resilience promise security; hidden and one perpetual place also limit mobility and public life. Both readings should use the image’s actual terms.
evidence: May she become a flourishing hidden tree

questions.prompt: Does rejecting hatred necessarily justify rejecting opinions?
facilitatorNotes: The poem moves from a persuasive warning about hatred to a much broader prescription against opinion. Readers may challenge that inference while recognizing the speaker’s personal disappointments and desire to protect.
evidence: So let her think opinions are accursed.

days.title: Demon and Beast
days.challenge: Follow a temporary experience while testing the speaker’s later explanation of it.
days.focus: Freedom from desire and the paradox of mastery.
days.context: The speaker experiences a brief release from hatred and desire. Gallery portraits, ordinary birds and ascetic figures become stages in his attempt to understand it.
days.contentNote: Religious asceticism and self-denial are invoked as historical images, not practical advice.

excerpt.locator: Demon and Beast; complete individual work; opens “For certain minutes at the least That crafty demon and that loud beast That plague me day and night ”; closes “ more Starved upon the shore And withered to a bag of bones: What had the Caesars but their thrones?”.

blocks.text:
For certain minutes at the least
That crafty demon and that loud beast
That plague me day and night
Ran out of my sight;
Though I had long pernned in the gyre,
Between my hatred and desire,
I saw my freedom won
And all laugh in the sun.

The glittering eyes in a death’s head
Of old Luke Wadding’s portrait said
Welcome, and the Ormonds all
Nodded upon the wall,
And even Stafford smiled as though
It made him happier to know
I understood his plan;
Now that the loud beast ran
There was no portrait in the Gallery
But beckoned to sweet company,
For all men’s thoughts grew clear
Being dear as mine are dear.

But soon a tear-drop started up
For aimless joy had made me stop
Beside the little lake
To watch a white gull take
A bit of bread thrown up into the air;
Now gyring down and pernning there
He splashed where an absurd
Portly green-pated bird
Shook off the water from his back;
Being no more demoniac
A stupid happy creature
Could rouse my whole nature.

Yet I am certain as can be
That every natural victory
Belongs to beast or demon,
That never yet had freeman
Right mastery of natural things,
And that mere growing old, that brings
Chilled blood, this sweetness brought;
Yet have no dearer thought
Than that I may find out a way
To make it linger half a day.

O what a sweetness strayed
Through barren Thebaid,
Or by the Mareotic sea
When that exultant Anthony
And twice a thousand more
Starved upon the shore
And withered to a bag of bones:
What had the Caesars but their thrones?

questions.prompt: What changes in the portraits when the demon and beast disappear?
facilitatorNotes: Formerly distant or contentious figures seem companionable because he can regard others’ thoughts as dear. The change is in his mode of attention, not in the paintings themselves.
evidence: For all men’s thoughts grew clear

questions.prompt: Why does the ordinary bird’s power matter beside the elevated gallery scene?
facilitatorNotes: An absurd, happy creature can move his whole nature without ambition or ideological agreement. The shift makes unguarded attention to ordinary life the test of his release.
evidence:
A stupid happy creature
Could rouse my whole nature.

questions.prompt: How does wanting to prolong freedom complicate the claim of freedom from desire?
facilitatorNotes: He desires the desireless state and suspects aging rather than chosen mastery caused it. The final ascetics suggest another possibility, but their bodily cost complicates triumph.
evidence: To make it linger half a day.

days.title: Towards Break of Day
days.challenge: Distinguish physical touch, memory and the uncertain sharing of dreams.
days.focus: Intimacy that cannot erase separate inward worlds.
days.context: Two sleepers approach waking. The speaker recalls a beloved waterfall and wonders whether the woman beside him has dreamed the same dream.

excerpt.locator: Towards Break of Day; complete individual work; opens “Was it the double of my dream The woman that by me lay Dreamed, or did we halve a dream Under the fi”; closes “terer sleep The marvellous stag of Arthur, That lofty white stag, leap From mountain steep to steep.”.

blocks.text:
Was it the double of my dream
The woman that by me lay
Dreamed, or did we halve a dream
Under the first cold gleam of day?

I thought “there is a waterfall
Upon Ben Bulban side,
That all my childhood counted dear;
Were I to travel far and wide
I could not find a thing so dear.”
My memories had magnified
So many times childish delight.

I would have touched it like a child
But knew my finger could but have touched
Cold stone and water. I grew wild
Even accusing heaven because
It had set down among its laws:
Nothing that we love over-much
Is ponderable to our touch.

I dreamed towards break of day,
The cold blown spray in my nostril.
But she that beside me lay
Had watched in bitterer sleep
The marvellous stag of Arthur,
That lofty white stag, leap
From mountain steep to steep.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker explain the waterfall’s incomparable value?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated memory enlarges childhood delight. Its value exceeds the physical object, which helps explain why touching stone and water would not recover the whole experience.
evidence:
My memories had magnified
So many times childish delight.

questions.prompt: Why accuse heaven over the limit of touch?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker experiences a mismatch between material contact and the immaterial intensity of love. The accusation turns disappointment into a proposed law of existence, which readers can question.
evidence:
Nothing that we love over-much
Is ponderable to our touch.

questions.prompt: Does the woman’s final dream answer the opening question?
facilitatorNotes: It provides a different image—the elusive white stag—and calls her sleep bitterer, suggesting analogous longing without identical experience. The relation remains partly inaccessible.
evidence: The marvellous stag of Arthur,

days.title: To Be Carved on a Stone at Ballylee
days.challenge: Develop a sustained reading of a six-line inscription through diction, form and future tense.
days.focus: Material restoration and the hoped-for survival of a name.
days.context: Read slowly several times, attending to the three rhymed pairs. The poem imagines its own words carved into the restored building.

excerpt.locator: To Be Carved on a Stone at Ballylee; complete individual work; opens “I, the poet William Yeats, With old mill boards and sea-green slates, And smithy work from the Gort ”; closes “Restored this tower for my wife George; And may these characters remain When all is ruin once again.”.

blocks.text:
I, the poet William Yeats,
With old mill boards and sea-green slates,
And smithy work from the Gort forge,
Restored this tower for my wife George;
And may these characters remain
When all is ruin once again.

questions.prompt: Why name old boards, local slates and forge work in a monument to a poet?
facilitatorNotes: The list grounds poetic self-commemoration in reused materials and communal craft. It records how the tower was restored instead of only praising its owner.
evidence: With old mill boards and sea-green slates,

questions.prompt: How do the opening self-identification and the gift to George distribute credit and purpose?
facilitatorNotes: The I foregrounds the poet’s authorship, but the restoration is for his wife and relies on named materials and labor. Discuss both self-inscription and domestic dedication.
evidence: Restored this tower for my wife George;

questions.prompt: What does once again do to the apparent permanence of a carved inscription?
facilitatorNotes: It places restoration within a cycle that includes renewed ruin. The may is a wish, not certainty: even durable words are asked to outlast the building’s present order.
evidence: When all is ruin once again.

days.title: The good-morrow
days.challenge: Reconstruct an argument that moves from awakening through geography to an impossible-sounding conclusion.
days.focus: Mutual love as an alternative scale of value.
days.context: The speaker addresses a lover at waking. Early modern spelling is retained; read the syntax before interpreting the geographical conceits.

excerpt.locator: The good-morrow.; complete individual work; opens “I WONDER by my troth, what thou, and I Did, till we lov'd? were we not wean'd till then? But suck'd ”; closes “equally; If our two loves be one, or, thou and I Love so alike, that none doe slacken, none can die.”.

blocks.text:
I WONDER by my troth, what thou, and I
Did, till we lov'd? were we not wean'd till then?
But suck'd on countrey pleasures, childishly?
Or snorted we in the seaven sleepers den?
T'was so; But this, all pleasures fancies bee.
If ever any beauty I did see,
Which I desir'd, and got, t'was but a dreame of thee.

And now good morrow to our waking soules,
Which watch not one another out of feare;
For love, all love of other sights controules,
And makes one little roome, an every where.
Let sea-discoverers to new worlds have gone,
Let Maps to other, worlds on worlds have showne,
Let us possesse one world, each hath one, and is one.

My face in thine eye, thine in mine appeares,
And true plaine hearts doe in the faces rest,
Where can we finde two better hemispheares
Without sharpe North, without declining West?
What ever dyes, was not mixt equally;
If our two loves be one, or, thou and I
Love so alike, that none doe slacken, none can die.

questions.prompt: What does the opening claim about infancy and sleep do to earlier pleasures?
facilitatorNotes: It retrospectively demotes them to preparation or dreams. This is the speaker’s totalizing claim for present love, not a neutral biography.
evidence: were we not wean'd till then?

questions.prompt: How can one room become everywhere without either lover traveling?
facilitatorNotes: Mutual attention gives the room the experiential completeness claimed for discovered worlds. The comparison competes with exploration while borrowing its language of possession.
evidence: And makes one little roome, an every where.

questions.prompt: What condition governs the promise that their love cannot die?
facilitatorNotes: The conclusion depends on equal mixture or equal love with no slackening. The conditional if leaves a vulnerability inside the confident promise.
evidence: If our two loves be one, or, thou and I

days.title: The Sunne Rising
days.challenge: Follow a speaker who changes tactics while pretending to command the cosmos.
days.focus: Hyperbole, intimacy and the appropriation of public power.
days.context: The lovers are interrupted by sunlight. The speaker first scolds the sun, then gives it a new job.
days.contentNote: An intimate bedroom address uses imperial and gendered assumptions as part of its extravagant rhetoric.

excerpt.locator: The Sunne Rising.; complete individual work; opens “BUSIE old foole, unruly Sunne, Why dost thou thus, Through windowes, and through curtaines call on u”; closes “ng us. Shine here to us, and thou art every where; This bed thy center is, these walls, thy spheare.”.

blocks.text:
BUSIE old foole, unruly Sunne,
Why dost thou thus,
Through windowes, and through curtaines call on us?
Must to thy motions lovers seasons run?
Sawcy pedantique wretch, goe chide
Late schoole boyes, and sowre prentices,
Goe tell Court-huntsmen, that the King will ride,
Call countrey ants to harvest offices;
Love, all alike, no season knowes, nor clyme,
Nor houres, dayes, moneths, which are the rags of time.

Thy beames, so reverend, and strong
Why shouldst thou thinke?
I could eclipse and cloud them with a winke,
But that I would not lose her sight so long:
If her eyes have not blinded thine,
Looke, and to morrow late, tell mee,
Whether both the'India's of spice and Myne
Be where thou leftst them, or lie here with mee.
Aske for those Kings whom thou saw'st yesterday,
And thou shalt heare, All here in one bed lay.

She'is all States, and all Princes, I,
Nothing else is.
Princes doe but play us; compar'd to this,
All honor's mimique; All wealth alchimie.
Thou sunne art halfe as happy'as wee,
In that the world's contracted thus;
Thine age askes ease, and since thy duties bee
To warme the world, that's done in warming us.
Shine here to us, and thou art every where;
This bed thy center is, these walls, thy spheare.

questions.prompt: How do schoolboys, apprentices and courtiers help define love’s imagined exemption?
facilitatorNotes: They belong to schedules and hierarchical duties; the speaker claims love lies beyond those measures. The scolding voice itself imitates an authority he rejects.
evidence: Nor houres, dayes, moneths, which are the rags of time.

questions.prompt: Why does the proposed wink fail as a demonstration of power over the sun?
facilitatorNotes: He can shut out its light but would also lose sight of the beloved. The boast exposes dependence and lets desire defeat the claimed mastery.
evidence: But that I would not lose her sight so long:

questions.prompt: Does the last stanza dismiss political hierarchy or reproduce it within the room?
facilitatorNotes: It dismisses external princes as imitations while assigning the woman states and the man princely power. The intimate world borrows the unequal structure it claims to surpass.
evidence: She'is all States, and all Princes, I,

days.title: The Canonization
days.challenge: Trace a defense that turns its accusers’ terms into a imagined future authority.
days.focus: The making of lovers into saints through poetry.
days.context: Canonization means recognition as a saint. The speaker applies religious and memorial language to an intimate relationship under criticism.
days.contentNote: Religious language is used provocatively to describe romantic and sexual union.

excerpt.locator: The Canonization.; complete individual work; opens “FOR Godsake hold your tongue, and let me love, Or chide my palsie, or my gout, My five gray haires, ”; closes “t they did all to you epitomize,) Countries, Townes, Courts: Beg from above A patterne of your love!”.

blocks.text:
FOR Godsake hold your tongue, and let me love,
Or chide my palsie, or my gout,
My five gray haires, or ruin'd fortune flout,
With wealth your state, your minde with Arts improve,
Take you a course, get you a place,
Observe his honour, or his grace,
Or the Kings reall, or his stamped face
Contemplate, what you will, approve,
So you will let me love.

Alas, alas, who's injur'd by my love?
What merchants ships have my sighs drown'd?
Who saies my teares have overflow'd his ground?
When did my colds a forward spring remove?
When did the heats which my veines fill
Adde one more to the plaguie Bill?
Soldiers finde warres, and Lawyers finde out still
Litigious men, which quarrels move,
Though she and I do love.

Call us what you will, wee are made such by love;
Call her one, mee another flye,
We'are Tapers too, and at our owne cost die,
And wee in us finde the'Eagle and the Dove.
The Phœnix ridle hath more wit
By us, we two being one, are it.
So to one neutrall thing both sexes fit,
Wee dye and rise the same, and prove
Mysterious by this love.

Wee can dye by it, if not live by love,
And if unfit for tombes and hearse
Our legend bee, it will be fit for verse;
And if no peece of Chronicle wee prove,
We'll build in sonnets pretty roomes;
As well a well wrought urne becomes
The greatest ashes, as halfe-acre tombes,
And by these hymnes, all shall approve
Us Canoniz'd for Love:

And thus invoke us; You whom reverend love
Made one anothers hermitage;
You, to whom love was peace, that now is rage;
Who did the whole worlds soule contract, and drove
Into the glasses of your eyes
(So made such mirrors, and such spies,
That they did all to you epitomize,)
Countries, Townes, Courts: Beg from above
A patterne of your love!

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza expose the absurdity of conventional love hyperbole?
facilitatorNotes: It asks whether sighs literally sink ships or tears flood property. By denying public harm, the speaker asks the critic to leave private love alone.
evidence: What merchants ships have my sighs drown'd?

questions.prompt: How do the phoenix and the two sexes challenge ordinary separation?
facilitatorNotes: The pair becomes one creature that dies and rises, making difference and union coexist. The poem calls this mysterious rather than explaining it through ordinary physical identity.
evidence: The Phœnix ridle hath more wit

questions.prompt: Why are sonnet rooms and an urn alternatives to chronicles and large tombs?
facilitatorNotes: Careful poetic form can preserve significance without public power or expensive scale. The poem performs the memorial it predicts and imagines later readers petitioning the lovers.
evidence: We'll build in sonnets pretty roomes;

days.title: Aire and Angels
days.challenge: Test a changing analogy whose conclusion introduces a new inequality.
days.focus: Embodied love and the limits of a supposedly spiritual argument.
days.context: The speaker moves among angels, bodies and an overloaded boat to explain where love can reside.
days.contentNote: The final comparison asserts a gender hierarchy that the discussion explicitly examines.

excerpt.locator: Aire and Angels.; complete individual work; opens “TWICE or thrice had I loved thee, Before I knew thy face or name; So in a voice, so in a shapelesse ”; closes “st such disparitie As is twixt Aire and Angells puritie, 'Twixt womens love, and mens will ever bee.”.

blocks.text:
TWICE or thrice had I loved thee,
Before I knew thy face or name;
So in a voice, so in a shapelesse flame,
Angells affect us oft, and worship'd bee;
Still when, to where thou wert, I came,
Some lovely glorious nothing I did see.
But since my soule, whose child love is,
Takes limmes of flesh, and else could nothing doe,
More subtile then the parent is,
Love must not be, but take a body too,
And therefore what thou wert, and who,
I bid Love aske, and now
That it assume thy body, I allow,
And fixe it selfe in thy lip, eye, and brow.

Whilst thus to ballast love, I thought,
And so more steddily to have gone,
With wares which would sinke admiration,
I saw, I had loves pinnace overfraught,
Ev'ry thy haire for love to worke upon
Is much too much, some fitter must be sought;
For, nor in nothing, nor in things
Extreme, and scatt'ring bright, can love inhere;
Then as an Angell, face, and wings
Of aire, not pure as it, yet pure doth weare,
So thy love may be my loves spheare;
Just such disparitie
As is twixt Aire and Angells puritie,
'Twixt womens love, and mens will ever bee.

questions.prompt: What problem does the first stanza identify in a wholly bodiless love?
facilitatorNotes: The soul needs limbs to act, so love likewise needs an embodied form. Lovely glorious nothing acknowledges attraction while questioning its capacity to become a relation.
evidence: Love must not be, but take a body too,

questions.prompt: Why does the boat require ballast and then become overburdened?
facilitatorNotes: Physical particularity should stabilize love, but fascination with every feature overwhelms it. The revision seeks an intermediate relation between abstraction and sheer sensory abundance.
evidence: I saw, I had loves pinnace overfraught,

questions.prompt: Does the final hierarchy between men’s and women’s love follow necessarily from the earlier need for embodiment?
facilitatorNotes: No; the angel/air analogy supplies a gendered assignment whose superiority is asserted. Students may explain the historical conceit while challenging the inference.
evidence: 'Twixt womens love, and mens will ever bee.

days.title: A Valediction: of weeping
days.challenge: Track tears through three distinct systems of comparison without treating them as literal events.
days.focus: Parting, reflected identity and emotional pressure.
days.context: A valediction is a farewell. The speaker transforms tears successively into coins, globes and threatening seas.

excerpt.locator: A Valediction: of weeping.; complete individual work; opens “LET me powre forth My teares before thy face, whil'st I stay here, For thy face coines them, and thy”; closes “ thou and I sigh one anothers breath, Who e'r sighes most, is cruellest, and hasts the others death.”.

blocks.text:
LET me powre forth
My teares before thy face, whil'st I stay here,
For thy face coines them, and thy stampe they beare,
And by this Mintage they are something worth,
For thus they bee
Pregnant of thee;
Fruits of much griefe they are, emblemes of more,
When a teare falls, that thou falst which it bore,
So thou and I are nothing then, when on a divers shore.

On a round ball
A workeman that hath copies by, can lay
An Europe, Afrique, and an Asia,
And quickly make that, which was nothing, All,
So doth each teare,
Which thee doth weare,
A globe, yea world by that impression grow,
Till thy teares mixt with mine doe overflow
This world, by waters sent from thee, my heaven dissolved so.

O more then Moone,
Draw not up seas to drowne me in thy spheare,
Weepe me not dead, in thine armes, but forbeare
To teach the sea, what it may doe too soone;
Let not the winde
Example finde,
To doe me more harme, then it purposeth;
Since thou and I sigh one anothers breath,
Who e'r sighes most, is cruellest, and hasts the others death.

questions.prompt: How does the beloved’s reflected face give the tears value?
facilitatorNotes: Like a stamped coin, a tear becomes precious by carrying her image. The image ties the speaker’s grief to recognition and the fear of losing her presence.
evidence: For thy face coines them, and thy stampe they beare,

questions.prompt: How does the globe comparison enlarge the stakes of a single falling tear?
facilitatorNotes: An image turns a small round surface into a world; mixed tears then threaten to dissolve that world. Scale magnifies emotional loss while exposing the conceit’s imaginative extravagance.
evidence: A globe, yea world by that impression grow,

questions.prompt: What change in the speaker’s attitude toward tears occurs by the final stanza?
facilitatorNotes: He begins asking permission to weep and ends asking the beloved to stop, linking her grief to danger. The supposed shared breath can sound intimate or emotionally coercive.
evidence: Who e'r sighes most, is cruellest, and hasts the others death.

days.title: The broken heart
days.challenge: Follow an argument whose successive comparisons change what survival means.
days.focus: The difference between continuing to feel and being able to love again.
days.context: The speaker rejects the idea that love simply lasts through ordinary time, then explains the fragmentary condition of his heart.
days.contentNote: Violent and disease imagery expresses emotional injury.

excerpt.locator: The broken heart.; complete individual work; opens “HE is starke mad, who ever sayes, That he hath beene in love an houre, Yet not that love so soone de”; closes “r faces, so My ragges of heart can like, wish, and adore, But after one such love, can love no more.”.

blocks.text:
HE is starke mad, who ever sayes,
That he hath beene in love an houre,
Yet not that love so soone decayes,
But that it can tenne in lesse space devour;
Who will beleeve mee, if I sweare
That I have had the plague a yeare?
Who would not laugh at mee, if I should say,
I saw a flaske of powder burne a day?

Ah, what a trifle is a heart,
If once into loves hands it come!
All other griefes allow a part
To other griefes, and aske themselves but some;
They come to us, but us Love draws,
Hee swallows us, and never chawes:
By him, as by chain'd shot, whole rankes doe dye,
He is the tyran Pike, our hearts the Frye.

If 'twere not so, what did become
Of my heart, when I first saw thee?
I brought a heart into the roome,
But from the roome, I carried none with mee:
If it had gone to thee, I know
Mine would have taught thine heart to show
More pitty unto mee: but Love, alas,
At one first blow did shiver it as glasse.

Yet nothing can to nothing fall,
Nor any place be empty quite,
Therefore I thinke my breast hath all
Those peeces still, though they be not unite;
And now as broken glasses show
A hundred lesser faces, so
My ragges of heart can like, wish, and adore,
But after one such love, can love no more.

questions.prompt: Why does saying love cannot last an hour not mean it is too brief or weak?
facilitatorNotes: Love is presented as so destructive that it can consume many hearts within that time. Plague and burning powder measure intensity rather than mere duration.
evidence: But that it can tenne in lesse space devour;

questions.prompt: How does the third stanza reject the usual idea that a lover gives away a heart?
facilitatorNotes: If the beloved possessed it, it would supposedly teach pity; because pity is absent, the speaker argues love shattered it instead. This is an emotionally interested inference, not proof about her inner life.
evidence: Mine would have taught thine heart to show

questions.prompt: What can the surviving fragments do that the whole heart once did differently?
facilitatorNotes: They can like, wish and adore but supposedly cannot unite in another total love. The mirror simile lets persistence coexist with damage and divided attention.
evidence: My ragges of heart can like, wish, and adore,

days.title: A Valediction: forbidding mourning
days.challenge: Compare successive analogies and notice how a conditional revises apparent certainty.
days.focus: A claim for continuity through physical separation.
days.context: The speaker asks for a quiet farewell, distinguishing their love from kinds dependent on immediate sensory presence.

excerpt.locator: A Valediction: forbidding mourning.; complete individual work; opens “AS virtuous men passe mildly away, And whisper to their soules, to goe, Whilst some of their sad fri”; closes “th'other foot, obliquely runne; Thy firmnes makes my circle just, And makes me end, where I begunne.”.

blocks.text:
AS virtuous men passe mildly away,
And whisper to their soules, to goe,
Whilst some of their sad friends doe say,
The breath goes now, and some say, no:

So let us melt, and make no noise,
No teare-floods, nor sigh-tempests move,
T'were prophanation of our joyes
To tell the layetie our love.

Moving of th'earth brings harmes and feares,
Men reckon what it did and meant,
But trepidation of the spheares,
Though greater farre, is innocent.

Dull sublunary lovers love
(Whose soule is sense) cannot admit
Absence, because it doth remove
Those things which elemented it.

But we by a love, so much refin'd,
That our selves know not what it is,
Inter-assured of the mind,
Care lesse, eyes, lips, and hands to misse.

Our two soules therefore, which are one,
Though I must goe, endure not yet
A breach, but an expansion,
Like gold to ayery thinnesse beate.

If they be two, they are two so
As stiffe twin compasses are two,
Thy soule the fixt foot, makes no show
To move, but doth, if the'other doe.

And though it in the center sit,
Yet when the other far doth rome,
It leanes, and hearkens after it,
And growes erect, as that comes home.

Such wilt thou be to mee, who must
Like th'other foot, obliquely runne;
Thy firmnes makes my circle just,
And makes me end, where I begunne.

questions.prompt: Why compare the farewell to the quiet death of virtuous people?
facilitatorNotes: The analogy values inward assurance over visible display. It may console, but also asks the listener to accept the speaker’s authority over how grief should be expressed.
evidence: So let us melt, and make no noise,

questions.prompt: How does beaten gold change separation from a breach into expansion?
facilitatorNotes: A continuous substance spreads thinner without breaking. It makes distance a change in form rather than loss of unity, though it remains a chosen image rather than a guarantee.
evidence: Like gold to ayery thinnesse beate.

questions.prompt: What does the fixed compass foot actually do, and why does that matter?
facilitatorNotes: It leans and responds as the other travels, so fixed does not mean inert. The eventual circle requires both partners; discuss whether the assigned roles remain unequal despite reciprocity.
evidence: It leanes, and hearkens after it,

days.title: The Extasie
days.challenge: Sustain attention through a long philosophical poem that argues back toward the body.
days.focus: Why spiritual intimacy still needs material expression.
days.context: Two lovers remain still and silent while the poem imagines their souls negotiating. The spelling extasie suggests a standing outside oneself.
days.contentNote: Philosophical discussion of romantic and bodily intimacy.

excerpt.locator: The Extasie.; complete individual work; opens “WHERE, like a pillow on a bed, A Pregnant banke swel'd up, to rest The violets reclining head, Sat w”; closes “this dialogue of one, Let him still marke us, he shall see Small change, when we'are to bodies gone.”.

blocks.text:
WHERE, like a pillow on a bed,
A Pregnant banke swel'd up, to rest
The violets reclining head,
Sat we two, one anothers best.
Our hands were firmely cimented
With a fast balme, which thence did spring,
Our eye-beames twisted, and did thred
Our eyes, upon one double string;
So to'entergraft our hands, as yet
Was all the meanes to make us one,
And pictures in our eyes to get
Was all our propagation.
As 'twixt two equall Armies, Fate
Suspends uncertaine victorie,
Our soules, (which to advance their state,
Were gone out,) hung 'twixt her, and mee.
And whil'st our soules negotiate there,
Wee like sepulchrall statues lay;
All day, the same our postures were,
And wee said nothing, all the day.
If any, so by love refin'd,
That he soules language understood,
And by good love were growen all minde,
Within convenient distance stood,
He (though he knew not which soule spake,
Because both meant, both spake the same)
Might thence a new concoction take,
And part farre purer then he came.
This Extasie doth unperplex
(We said) and tell us what we love,
Wee see by this, it was not sexe,
Wee see, we saw not what did move:
But as all severall soules containe
Mixture of things, they know not what,
Love, these mixt soules, doth mixe againe,
And makes both one, each this and that.
A single violet transplant,
The strength, the colour, and the size,
(All which before was poore, and scant,)
Redoubles still, and multiplies.
When love, with one another so
Interinanimates two soules,
That abler soule, which thence doth flow,
Defects of lonelinesse controules.
Wee then, who are this new soule, know,
Of what we are compos'd, and made,
For, th'Atomies of which we grow,
Are soules, whom no change can invade.
But O alas, so long, so farre
Our bodies why doe wee forbeare?
They are ours, though they are not wee, Wee are
The intelligences, they the spheare.
We owe them thankes, because they thus,
Did us, to us, at first convay,
Yeelded their forces, sense, to us,
Nor are drosse to us, but allay.
On man heavens influence workes not so,
But that it first imprints the ayre,
Soe soule into the soule may flow,
Though it to body first repaire.
As our blood labours to beget
Spirits, as like soules as it can,
Because such fingers need to knit
That subtile knot, which makes us man:
So must pure lovers soules descend
T'affections, and to faculties,
Which sense may reach and apprehend,
Else a great Prince in prison lies.
To'our bodies turne wee then, that so
Weake men on love reveal'd may looke;
Loves mysteries in soules doe grow,
But yet the body is his booke.
And if some lover, such as wee,
Have heard this dialogue of one,
Let him still marke us, he shall see
Small change, when we'are to bodies gone.

facilitatorNotes: Hands, eye-beams, the swelling bank and violets make sensory contact foundational. The souls’ departure depends on a scene of embodied intimacy.

questions.prompt: What does the transplanted violet explain about the lovers’ supposed new soul?
facilitatorNotes: Transplanting strengthens and enlarges the living plant; their union similarly transforms existing mixtures. The analogy suggests mutual enhancement rather than the simple erasure of two identities.
evidence: A single violet transplant,

questions.prompt: Why does the poem finally call the body a book rather than dross?
facilitatorNotes: Embodiment communicates inward love to the lovers and witnesses. Calling it alloy also grants an enabling function; the ending argues that spirit needs expression rather than despising matter.
evidence: But yet the body is his booke.

days.title: A Lecture upon the Shadow
days.challenge: Test the fit and limits of a natural process used as an argument about love.
days.focus: Disclosure, self-deception and a demand for permanence.
days.context: A speaker turns a walk near noon into a lesson addressed to a lover. Sunlight supplies the poem’s model and its central difficulty.

excerpt.locator: A Lecture upon the Shadow.; complete individual work; opens “STAND still, and I will read to thee A Lecture, Love, in loves philosophy. These three houres that w”; closes “Love is a growing, or full constant light; And his first minute, after noone, is night.”.

blocks.text:
STAND still, and I will read to thee
A Lecture, Love, in loves philosophy.
These three houres that we have spent,
Walking here, Two shadowes went
Along with us, which we our selves produc'd;
But, now the Sunne is just above our head,
We doe those shadowes tread;
And to brave clearnesse all things are reduc'd.
So whilst our infant loves did grow,
Disguises did, and shadowes, flow,
From us, and our cares; but, now 'tis not so.

That love hath not attain'd the high'st degree,
Which is still diligent lest others see.

Except our loves at this noone stay,
We shall new shadowes make the other way.
As the first were made to blinde
Others; these which come behinde
Will worke upon our selves, and blind our eyes.
If our loves faint, and westwardly decline;
To me thou, falsly, thine,
And I to thee mine actions shall disguise.
The morning shadowes weare away,
But these grow longer all the day,
But oh, loves day is short, if love decay.

Love is a growing, or full constant light;
And his first minute, after noone, is night.

questions.prompt: What do the morning shadows correspond to in the early relationship?
facilitatorNotes: Disguises and concern about other observers; the couple itself produces them. The noon image imagines clarity achieved by standing over those earlier shadows.
evidence: Disguises did, and shadowes, flow,

questions.prompt: How do the later shadows differ from the earlier ones?
facilitatorNotes: The earlier disguises blind outsiders; later ones would blind the lovers themselves. Decline therefore changes secrecy from mutual protection into mutual deception.
evidence: Will worke upon our selves, and blind our eyes.

questions.prompt: What tension does the wish to remain at noon introduce into the lecture’s natural analogy?
facilitatorNotes: The sun cannot physically remain at noon, but love is asked to maintain fullness. The final sudden night abandons gradual natural time for an absolute emotional standard.
evidence: And his first minute, after noone, is night.

days.challenge: Attend to the changing refrain and sound-play while reconstructing the prayer’s sequence.
days.focus: Confession, recurring fault and assurance.

blocks.text:
WILT thou forgive that sinne where I begunne,
Which was my sin, though it were done before?
Wilt thou forgive that sinne; through which I runne,
And do run still: though still I do deplore?
When thou hast done, thou hast not done,
For, I have more.

Wilt thou forgive that sinne which I have wonne
Others to sinne? and, made my sinne their doore?
Wilt thou forgive that sinne which I did shunne
A yeare, or two: but wallowed in, a score?
When thou hast done, thou hast not done,
For I have more.

questions.prompt: Why does the first question distinguish a sin that was his from one done before?
facilitatorNotes: It invokes inherited sin while insisting on personal involvement, then shifts to acts still repeated despite remorse. The distinction prevents confession from being only a list of completed events.

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza widen responsibility beyond the speaker’s own actions?
facilitatorNotes: He has made sin an entryway for others and returned to practices once avoided. The continuing refrain registers unfinished reckoning rather than a quick discharge of guilt.
evidence: made my sinne their doore?
